title: Comparing and choosing
job: More, less, better — stating a preference
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: A comparison is an ENDING on the thing you are comparing against. phalāt jalam varam is 'water is better than fruit' — literally 'from fruit, water is better'. The -āt on phalāt is the whole of 'than', and it sits on the noun English would put last.

There is no word for 'than' anywhere on this page, and looking for one is the first thing an English speaker does. English hands you a signal word in the middle of the sentence; this language hands you an ending at the START of it, on the wrong noun, and nothing else.

A grammar makes comparatives with the suffixes -tara and -tama, the way English makes them with -er and -est. They are real and this course writes neither. Everyday speech compares with the ablative and with adhikam, and a suffix paradigm would be a second system inside a module that already opens a case.

This module opens the ablative on exactly two words — phalāt and jalāt — and the rule carries the rest. Every ablative of every noun would be a separate surface, and two written shapes with a rule beside them teach more than six written shapes with none. M4's instrumental was opened the same way and for the same reason.

adhikam is 'more'. It stands in front of what there is more of — adhikam jalam, 'more water' — and in front of a verb it means more of the doing: adhikam paṭhati is 'reads more'. It is an ordinary a-stem word, so on a neuter noun it ends -am like every other adjective M3 taught.

alpam is the other end of the same scale: 'a little', 'not much'. alpam jalam is a small quantity of water, and it is the polite way to accept an offer you do not want much of — M5's alam refuses it altogether.

The preference frame is M1's, four modules into a second level: mahyam dugdham adhikam rocate is 'milk is more pleasing to me'. The thing preferred is still the subject and you are still only the person it pleases, and adhikam does the comparing without disturbing any of that.

vā is 'or', and it comes AFTER the second choice: pustakam phalam vā is 'a book or a fruit'. That is the same placement law M10 taught for ca and M6 taught for saha, so there is nothing new to learn about where it goes — only that it goes there.

varam is 'better' and nothing else in this course. It is an indeclinable word rather than an adjective, so it never agrees with anything: jalam varam, dugdham varam, phalam varam, all with the same shape.

Word order carries the comparison, so the ablative goes FIRST. phalāt jalam varam, not jalam phalāt varam. The second is understandable and the first is what a speaker says, and the literal line under each sentence is there to keep the order visible.

words.note: M1's fruit in the from-shape. That row shipped phalam alone, so this is a new row for a word the course has had since its first module, and the -āt is the whole of English 'than'.
'Better'. It never changes shape for what it describes, which makes it the easiest word in a module whose other half is a case ending.
M3's water in its plain naming shape — it is the thing that IS better, and so it is the subject. Only the other noun moved.

sentences.trap: English puts the word 'than' in the middle and the compared thing at the end. Here the compared thing comes FIRST, carries the whole comparison in its ending, and there is no middle word at all.
sentences.sound: pha-LAAT JA-lam VA-ram. phalāt ends in a hard t; the -āt is long and clipped off sharply.

variations.changed: what is better changes, and the from-shape on the fruit does not
the two nouns swap jobs, so the ending swaps with them — this is the clearest proof that the -āt is the comparison
the comparison is dropped for a plain preference, using M1's frame and no ending at all

mistake.why: The fruit has been left in its naming shape, which makes the sentence two subjects and a 'better' with nothing to lean on. The thing compared AGAINST must carry the -āt, and it is the only marker the comparison has.

sentences.usage: Said about what to have, and said without any softening — a preference in this language is stated flatly.
sentences.mnemonic: The loser takes the ending. Whatever you are comparing AGAINST is the word that changes, and it goes first.

words.note: M3's water in the from-shape, and the module's second and last written ablative. Every other noun's ablative is made the same way and this course writes none of them.
The same shape as in the sentence before, beside a different noun. Nothing about varam ever moves, which is why the ending on the first word has to carry the work.
M5's milk, and the subject here. In that module it appeared as dugdhena, the thing refused; the plain shape is the thing being praised.

sentences.sound: ja-LAAT DUG-dham VA-ram. The -gdh- of dugdham is one cluster and both consonants are voiced.

variations.display: jalāt dugdham varam, kintu aham jalam icchāmi.
variations.script: जलात् दुग्धम् वरम्, किन्तु अहम् जलम् इच्छामि।
variations.cue: Milk is better than water, but I want water.
variations.changed: M10's kintu hangs a preference on the end that contradicts the comparison, which is a thing people do constantly
M5's annam takes the subject slot, and the from-shape stays where it was
the thing compared against is left unsaid, which is what happens when everybody already knows what it is

sentences.usage: The second half of a choice, said once the first option is on the table.

sentences.cue: I want a book or a fruit.

words.note: 'Or', and it comes AFTER the second choice. M2 named this word as a thing the course had not written yet; this is where it arrives, and it arrives in one reading only.
M3's wanting verb at the end, where a verb goes. Both choices in front of it take the same shape, because both are equally the thing wanted.
M1's book as the thing wanted. Two things offered as alternatives are simply set beside each other, with vā after the second.

sentences.trap: vā is where English puts nothing. 'A book or a fruit' has its 'or' between the two, and here the word sits behind them both — the same place ca sits, and the same place api sits.
sentences.sound: a-HAM PUS-ta-kam PHA-lam VAA IC-chhaa-mi. vā is a single long beat and is never stressed.

variations.cue: I want a book or a fruit.
variations.changed: aham drops, which is the ordinary shape — the -mi has already said who wants

variations.cue: I want a book and a fruit.
variations.changed: M10's ca takes vā's exact place and asks for both instead of either — two words, one slot, opposite meanings
the pair of choices changes and vā stays behind the second of them

mistake.why: vā has been put where English puts 'or'. It is postpositive: it follows the second of the things it joins, exactly as ca does, and this is the single commonest slip an English speaker makes with all three of these little words.

sentences.usage: Ordering, and the most useful sentence in the module.

words.note: 'More', standing in front of the verb and saying more of the pleasing. It is an ordinary a-stem word, so it ends -am beside a neuter noun or a verb.
M1's liking verb, still agreeing with the milk rather than with me. Nine modules on, the frame has not straightened out and it will not.
Here as mahyam, 'to me' — the shape the liking frame has wanted since M1. Comparison has changed nothing about which word is the subject.

sentences.trap: 'I like milk more' has the person as the subject in English and as an afterthought here. The milk is doing the pleasing, and adhikam only says how much of it there is.
sentences.sound: MAH-yam DUG-dham a-DHI-kam RO-cha-te. adhikam is three even beats; the dh is a d with breath behind it.

variations.changed: the thing preferred changes and nothing else in the frame does
M5's bhavate takes mahyam's place, and the person pleased becomes the guest
more than one thing pleases, so M9's rocante replaces rocate — and adhikam, which agrees with nothing, does not move

mistake.why: adhikataram is a real comparative, built with the -tara suffix a grammar teaches. This course writes no -tara and no -tama anywhere: comparison here is the ablative and adhikam, and nothing else.

sentences.usage: A preference given when two things have already been named, which is when 'more' means anything at all.

words.note: In front of a noun now rather than a verb: more OF the water. It ends -am because jalam is neuter, exactly as M3's adjectives did.
M3's wanting, unchanged. What has changed is only how much is wanted, and that is one word in front of the noun.
The thing wanted, in the shape it has had since M3. Notice this is NOT M5's punaḥ — 'more water' and 'drink again' are two different sentences.

sentences.trap: M5 taught punaḥ pibatu for 'have some more'. That is 'drink again' and belongs to the verb; adhikam jalam is 'a greater quantity of water' and belongs to the noun. English uses 'more' for both.

variations.changed: M5's food takes the slot, also neuter, so the -am on adhikam stays
the other end of the scale, in the same slot and with the same ending
the host asks instead of the guest saying, so kim goes in front and the ending moves to -ti

sentences.usage: Asked at a table, and the honest answer to M5's second offer.

sentences.cue: Please give me a little water.

words.note: 'A little'. It is adhikam's opposite and sits in exactly the same slot with exactly the same ending — one scale, two words, no new machinery.
M3's 'please give', which this course has had since its third module. Asking for a small amount needs no verb of its own.
The thing asked for. alpam agrees with it in the same way any adjective does, which is why the two words look alike.

sentences.trap: alpam is not a refusal. M5's alam declines the whole offer; alpam accepts a small part of it, and the two words are one letter apart and opposite in effect.
sentences.sound: kri-PA-yaa AL-pam JA-lam da-DAA-tu. alpam and alam differ by one consonant and it is worth saying both aloud.

variations.cue: Please give me a little milk.
variations.changed: milk instead of water, with both words in front of it unchanged

variations.cue: Please give me a little water.
variations.changed: kṛpayā drops and the request keeps its courtesy, which lives in the -tu

variations.cue: No more water. I would like a little milk.
variations.changed: M5's refusal and this module's small acceptance stand side by side, which is the clearest way to hear the difference

sentences.usage: The polite middle between taking a full glass and refusing one.

sentences.display: kim bhavān jalam dugdham vā icchati?
sentences.script: किम् भवान् जलम् दुग्धम् वा इच्छति?
sentences.cue: Would you like water or milk?

words.note: Behind the second choice again, inside a question this time. Its position does not change because the sentence became a question.
Here as icchati, because it is the guest who wants. M3 shipped both shapes on this one row and this module uses each of them once.
The polite 'you' with its third-person verb, which is the register the whole course speaks. Offering a choice does not change it.

sentences.trap: There are two question markers' worth of work here and only one word doing it. kim makes the whole thing a question; vā makes the two nouns alternatives. Neither can do the other's job.
sentences.sound: KIM bha-VAAN JA-lam DUG-dham VAA IC-chha-ti. The list rises on jalam and falls after vā.

variations.display: kim bhavatī jalam dugdham vā icchati?
variations.script: किम् भवती जलम् दुग्धम् वा इच्छति?
variations.cue: Would you like water or milk?
variations.changed: asked of a woman; only the address forks and the verb does not

variations.display: kim bhavān pustakam phalam vā icchati?
variations.script: किम् भवान् पुस्तकम् फलम् वा इच्छति?
variations.cue: Would you like a book or a fruit?
variations.changed: the pair of choices changes and the shape of the offer does not
the answer, which names one of the two and drops vā entirely

mistake.display: kim bhavān jalam vā dugdham icchati?
mistake.why: vā has slid in between the two choices, where English puts 'or'. It belongs after the SECOND of them — jalam dugdham vā — and putting it in the middle is the same slip as putting ca in the middle.

sentences.usage: What a host asks, and the question M5's module could not yet build.

words.note: 'More' as the whole predicate: the price is more than it ought to be. Three words with no verb between them are a complete sentence, as they have been since M1.
M8's price. It is neuter, which is why adhikam ends -am — the agreement M3 taught is doing the work here with no adjective in sight.
M1's 'this', in front of a neuter noun as always. All three words in this sentence end -am and all three are neuter, which is not a coincidence.

sentences.trap: English needs 'too' and this sentence has no word for it. adhikam is simply 'more', and what it is more THAN is left to the room — which is exactly how a complaint about a price is made.

variations.changed: M3's asti is written out, which is heavier and means exactly the same thing
the other end of the scale, in the same slot and with the same ending

variations.cue: The price of the fruit is too high.
variations.changed: M7's 'of the fruit' says whose price it is, and the comparison at the end is untouched

mistake.why: mūlyam is neuter, so anything said about it ends -am. adhikaḥ is the shape a masculine word would take, and this course writes only the neuter one.

sentences.usage: Said at a stall, and about as close to haggling as this course goes.

words.note: In front of a verb, saying more of the reading rather than more of a thing. Its shape does not change to do this, which is why it can stand in both places.
M4's verb of reading. It is the amount of reading that is being compared, and the verb itself is unchanged by that.
M2's brother, in his naming shape as the subject. Notice he is not compared with anybody — 'more' can stand with nothing after it.

variations.changed: a sister instead of a brother, and adhikam does not fork because it never agrees with a subject
the reader becomes the speaker, so the verb takes -mi
less instead of more, in the same slot with the same shape

sentences.usage: Said in comparison with somebody who is standing right there, and the comparison is left unspoken.

sentences.display: jalāt dugdham varam, ataḥ aham dugdham icchāmi.
sentences.script: जलात् दुग्धम् वरम्, अतः अहम् दुग्धम् इच्छामि।
sentences.cue: Milk is better than water, so I want milk.
sentences.literal: from-water milk better, so I milk want

words.note: The judgement in the first half, with the choice following from it in the second. That is the whole shape of this module's job.
The from-shape at the front, where the comparison always starts. The same noun appears twice in this sentence and only the first one carries an ending.
M9's 'so', joining a judgement to the choice that follows from it. It is the one word in this module that has to stand at the FRONT of its clause.

sentences.trap: dugdham appears twice and looks identical both times, but the first is the thing judged better and the second is the thing wanted. Only jalāt moved, because only it is being compared against.
sentences.sound: ja-LAAT DUG-dham VA-ram, A-tah a-HAM DUG-dham IC-chhaa-mi. There is a real pause at the comma and ataḥ starts the second half.

variations.display: phalāt jalam varam, ataḥ aham jalam pibāmi.
variations.script: फलात् जलम् वरम्, अतः अहम् जलम् पिबामि।
variations.cue: Water is better than fruit, so I drink water.
variations.changed: the whole comparison changes and the shape of the two halves does not

variations.display: jalāt dugdham varam, kintu aham jalam icchāmi.
variations.script: जलात् दुग्धम् वरम्, किन्तु अहम् जलम् इच्छामि।
variations.cue: Milk is better than water, but I want water.
variations.changed: M10's kintu replaces ataḥ, and the second half now contradicts the first instead of following from it
the consequence drops and the judgement stands alone

sentences.usage: The module in one line: a comparison, and the choice it leads to.
sentences.mnemonic: varam names the winner, -āt marks the loser, and ataḥ says what you are going to do about it.
